open_obligations: Check whether the setup counts as sandwiching given that experts are humans, not a model more capable than the non-experts.
Note that no model is trained or aligned in the inner loop.
Check how ground-truth labels are used for evaluation versus Bowman et al.'s expert outer loop.
out.other_title: Do debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling work in sandwiching trials?
out.rationale: Bowman et al. call for empirical trials of debate under sandwiching. Michael et al. have non-expert judges who cannot read the passage judge debates between experts who can, reporting 84% for debate versus 74% for consultancy; the 'model' is often a human expert and there is no fine-tuning loop, so it is a relaxed sandwiching test.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps non-experts supervise better-informed experts, in a sandwiching-like setup on QuALITY-hard

open_obligations: Check that the expertise gap (hidden passage) is a fair stand-in for the capability gap Irving et al. target.
Check whether the debaters were trained toward equilibrium; if not, the result is about judge usability, not equilibrium behaviour.
Check whether the paper reports an upper bound on judge accuracy, and how it was computed, before reading the 84% as near-ceiling.
out.other_title: Debate is a proposal only for natural language; theory assumes error-free judges
out.rationale: Irving et al. state debate had only an MNIST demonstration and that significant research is needed to know whether it works with human judges. Michael et al. report human-debater debates judged by non-expert humans reach 84% accuracy versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage; the paper also compares human with AI debaters.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate works in practice with human judges in natural language, on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage

open_obligations: Note that Michael et al. compare debate with consultancy, not with a no-argument or single-turn condition.
Note that hiding the passage changes what the arguments must supply.
Check which design change (turns, interaction, hidden passage, debater skill) drives the difference.

Check whether Michael et al.'s debaters' counterarguments explicitly reference deficiencies in the other argument, as Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on; the cited passage says only that debaters are expected to defend their position against criticism.
out.other_title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
out.rationale: Parrish et al. ask whether a multi-turn setting with explicit counterarguments is needed for debate to help. Michael et al. contrast their setting with the one- and two-turn debates of Parrish et al., in which debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy: their debates are unbounded in length, and debaters are expected to defend their position against criticism by their opponent for as long as the judge is not convinced of the answer. They report 84% judge accuracy for debate versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions; their judges have not read the source passage and see only expert arguments and short quotes selectively revealed by the debaters, and debaters are expert humans, so several factors differ.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether unbounded multi-turn debate helps human judges on hard reading comprehension questions

open_obligations: Check which design difference (hidden passage, interaction, baseline) explains the different conclusions.
Note that Michael et al. have no no-argument baseline, so the two results answer different comparisons.
Check that both use QuALITY questions of comparable difficulty (hard subsets).
out.other_title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments did not help humans on the authors' reading comprehension task
out.rationale: Parrish et al. conclude that, for reading comprehension, debate is not a helpful format, since judges perform similarly with or without two-turn arguments. Michael et al. report 84% judge accuracy for interactive human debate versus 74% for consultancy on QuALITY-hard; settings differ sharply: Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage, debates are interactive and unbounded, and the baseline is consultancy rather than no arguments.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate is a helpful format for human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension

state_meaning: AI-drafted candidate; no person has reviewed it.
text: The authors report that, on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage, human-written debates between two expert debaters (one arguing for the correct answer, the other for an incorrect one) yield 84% judge accuracy versus 74% for consultancy, where a single expert argues for only one answer which is correct half of the time; debates are also 68% of the length of consultancies. Comparing human to AI debaters, they report evidence that with more skilled (in this case, human) debaters, debate performance goes up while consultancy performance goes down.
title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert judges: 84% vs 74% on hard reading comprehension questions
